accuracy.evidence: Curriculum placement checked against the GCSE Mathematics subject content (DfE 2013: infer properties of populations from a sample, knowing the limitations of sampling), Common Core 7.SP.A.1 and HSS-IC.B.3. The bias types follow standard definitions (selection or sampling bias, voluntary-response and convenience samples, response bias from question wording, non-response bias) as in Moore, McCabe and Craig's Introduction to the Practice of Statistics. Every lab figure was recomputed from the stated model: 0.4 x 0.85 + 0.6 x 0.3 = 52%; skate shop 0.95 x 0.85 + 0.05 x 0.3 = 82.25%; library 35.5%; reply rates 20% and 60% give 0.176 / 0.44 = 40%; the faulty plan gives 92.5%. The 1936 Literary Digest poll (about 2.4 million replies, wrong winner) matches Squire (1988). The lesson says plainly that the town is a model, not survey data.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented errors in students' reasoning about samples: believing a large sample cannot be biased (step 1 prediction '200 is plenty', step 3 'send 5,000 forms', challenge 'big', 'size', 'tenth', m10), believing wording cannot change answers (step 2 prediction), believing any random sample is unbiased whatever the replies (challenge 'random'), confusing the three sources (sort step, challenge 'frame', 'word'), and treating volunteers or first-come samples as fair ('vol', 'gate').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsurvey models one town with two groups and computes the expected survey result from teen share, wording shift and group reply rates: a stand dragged between three places with a who-was-asked bar, three wording slots that toggle between loaded and neutral, two draggable reply-rate columns with a ten-times-the-forms switch, a three-way bias sort and a three-fault plan. flagsample covers population vs sample and random-sample spread; flagbias (personal biases, ages 9-11) is unrelated. lab_distinct passed under 30% against every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner moves things and the numbers answer: the skate shop returns '95% of the people asked are teens, but the town is 40% teens. The survey says 82%, too high by 30 points', each neutral phrase drops the result by 5 points with the same people, and the 10x switch reports 'Still 40%: more forms do not fix who replies' until the reply rates are equal. The plan step shows that fixing only one fault leaves the estimate wrong ('2 faults left: each kind of bias needs its own fix').

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each have a tempting wrong option that the lab disproves: '200 is plenty' (the skate shop gives 82% against a census of 52%), 'the yes share stays the same' when only wording changes (67% falls to 52% as phrases are made neutral), and '5,000 forms gets close to 52%' (the estimate stays at 40% at either size). The reveal line repeats the learner's choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Twelve distinct wrong-answer messages across six rotating questions: big sample assumed safe (big), wording blamed for a place fault (word), two leading wordings explained (lead, lead2), non-response mistaken for sampling bias (frame), random assumed enough (random), bias thought to vanish or shrink with size (size, tenth), question length blamed (short), reply count blamed instead of who replies (few), convenience sample (gate) and volunteers (vol).

readability.evidence: Learner paragraphs keep to short sentences with one idea each and stay inside the learner readability limit the validator enforces; they define bias as 'a fault in the method that pushes the answer the same way every time'. The adult text uses the precise terms sampling (selection) bias, convenience sample, voluntary response, leading or loaded question, non-response bias, systematic vs random error and representative sample. Canvas labels are 12-15 px with one line of prompt.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no banned phrases and explanation overlap stayed under 12% against every lesson, including Populations and samples (502) and Questioning Your Own Biases (322). Every feedback line states a number or names the fault ('Too few teen replies, so the result is too low'); there are no warm-up sentences.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 light and dark and 360 px Android dark screenshots of every step: the three place cards fit in one row with wrapped labels, the gauge label was moved above the bar after it collided with the census marker, the reply-rate columns are 64 px wide with their percentages inside, the three bias boxes show their counts, and the plan rows keep two 13 px chips per row. Real touch drags on iPhone 13 moved the stand to the skate shop and the random list, dragged the teens column to 70% and 30%, and dropped two survey cards into their boxes.

accessibility.evidence: The walkthrough gate completed all five tasks with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge showed, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in light or dark. Every drag has a labelled button ('Put the survey stand at: Skate shop', 'Teens reply rate up 10 points', 'Send 10x forms', 'This survey's fault: Who replies (non-response)', 'Wording: Neutral'), and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with every result so the numbers are read out.
